opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so there were a few reasons. The main one is practical: for each impossible language we wanted to train GPT-2-style models from scratch, and we had a whole set of languages: shuffled word orders, reversed sentences, count-based grammar rules, and so on. Training on something like the full web-scale datasets that modern LLMs see just wasn't feasible for that many conditions, and honestly it wasn't necessary to answer the question we were asking.

BabyLM is around 100 million words, which is in the ballpark of what a child might be exposed to by early adolescence. So it's a developmentally plausible amount of data, and that ties nicely into the framing of the debate. Chomsky and others have made claims about what humans can and can't learn, and about whether language models are informative about human language acquisition. If you're going to make comparisons to human learning, it's at least somewhat more reasonable to do it at a data scale closer to what humans actually experience, rather than trillions of tokens.

The other nice thing is that the corpus is pretty diverse: child-directed speech, transcribed conversation, children's books, some Wikipedia, subtitles. So it isn't one narrow domain. And because it's a shared benchmark that the community already uses, it gives a common reference point. Other people working on data-efficient learning are using the same data, so our results can sit alongside that line of work.

And importantly, since we apply our perturbations to the same base corpus, every impossible language is matched to the natural English baseline in vocabulary and content. The only thing changing is the structural rule we impose, which makes for a clean controlled comparison.

r001.rationale: The response describes BabyLM’s roughly 100 million words as a developmentally plausible amount, comparable to what a child encounters by early adolescence, connecting its scale to child language learning.

r002.rationale: It says each impossible language is derived by applying perturbations to the same base corpus and that only the structural rule changes, enabling a controlled comparison.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the BabyLM corpus was really appealing to us for a few reasons. The big one is scale. The whole premise of the BabyLM challenge is to ask what you can learn from roughly the amount of linguistic input a child gets, so the corpus is on the order of 100 million words. That's small enough that we could actually afford to train a lot of models from scratch, which is essential for this kind of work. We weren't fine-tuning one pretrained model; we were training separate GPT-2 style models on each of our impossible languages, plus the natural English baseline, across multiple random seeds. If we'd tried to do that at the scale of something like The Pile, it just wouldn't have been feasible.

The second reason is that it's clean, natural English that's reasonably child-directed or at least developmentally plausible. It's a mix of transcribed speech, children's books, simple Wikipedia, subtitles, that kind of thing. For our purposes we really wanted the starting data to be unambiguously a real human language, so that when we applied our perturbations, whether that's shuffling words, reversing sentences, or adding our count-based verb marking, the only thing changing was the structure we were manipulating. Everything else about the content and vocabulary stays constant, so the comparison between the possible and impossible versions is as controlled as we could make it.

And then there's a conceptual connection too. Part of what motivated the whole project was this claim, which Chomsky and others have made, that language models can learn possible and impossible languages equally well, and therefore can't tell us anything about human language. The BabyLM setting is explicitly framed around comparing models to human learners under human-like data constraints, so it felt like the right arena to actually test that claim in. If models trained on child-scale data still show a clear preference for natural English over the impossible variants, that's a much more meaningful result than if you had to throw trillions of tokens at the problem to see any difference.

r001.rationale: The response connects BabyLM to child-scale linguistic input, but does not communicate the specific first-12-years approximation in the criterion.

r002.rationale: It says the perturbations are applied to the same starting English data, keeping content and vocabulary constant so comparisons among the variants are controlled.

astra-6.text:
The appeal of BabyLM is that it gives us a way to study learning at a more human-like scale. Children acquire language from much less input than the enormous amounts of text we typically use to train language models, and BabyLM was designed to bring the training setting closer to that constraint. It also includes a substantial amount of conversational speech, which is relevant to the kinds of input children receive.

For our experiments, we can take that corpus and systematically transform it to create our impossible languages. That gives us a controlled comparison: we keep the underlying content and the amount of training data the same, but change particular properties of the language. Then we can ask whether a model finds those transformed languages harder to learn than the original, rather than having differences in the data obscure that comparison.

r001.rationale: The response says BabyLM brings training closer to children’s input constraints and includes conversational speech, but does not connect its design to approximating the input a child encounters during the first 12 years of life.

r002.rationale: It explains that transforming the same corpus while keeping the underlying content and data amount constant enables controlled comparisons among the original and transformed languages.

sol-6.1.text:
The idea is to ask whether language models have a harder time learning languages that humans couldn’t naturally acquire. BabyLM gives us a useful starting point because it’s a relatively small corpus designed to approximate the amount and kind of language a child might encounter, with a lot of conversational text.

That lets us take the same underlying data and systematically transform it to introduce these impossible grammatical rules. We can then compare learning on the original corpus with learning on the transformed versions, while keeping the vocabulary and content largely the same. And because the dataset is relatively small, we can train models from scratch across multiple conditions, rather than starting with a model that already knows a natural language.

r001.rationale: It says BabyLM approximates the amount and kind of language a child might encounter, but does not specify the first 12 years of life.

r002.rationale: It describes transforming the same underlying data into different versions and comparing them with the original, which communicates controlled comparisons from a shared corpus.
